<reason>Both sides were strong and grounded, with clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 compliance and no fake sourcing. A built a real case (de facto ban, contextual yield gap, regressive paywalls, proportionality of presumptive illegality) and answered pressure honestly. But B won the central thread: it answered both pressure questions with workable specifications (refusal must be real; a cross-context scale line with the duty on the network, not the publisher) and, decisively, converted A's own concessions — friction, pennies, rational ignorance — into the affirmative argument that individuals can never carry the opt-out burden, which is exactly the case for an ex ante presumption. A's proportionality counter was sharp but met by B's takings frame and the two-decades-of-failed-ex-post point. Execution also favored B: A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the limit, A4.2 misdescribed B's frictionless-consent question as a concession, and A's closing overclaimed that "both agree" opt-in collapses. B's "who acts first" crystallization made the decision cleaner.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's turn of A's "friction, not revulsion" concession: if data flows only because refusal is costly and each harm is worth pennies, then opt-out can never work and smallness does not license taking — capped by "we don't ask the wiretapper to prove the call mattered," which neutralized A's unproven-harm inversion and reframed the presumption as answering the taking itself.</best_rebuttal>
